claim: Joint held-out prediction on control trials favored the tested accumulator over a rapid-forgetting implementation, but randomized motion pulses exposed a failure of the tested model-and-input pipelines to generalize to transient strong evidence.
note: Single out-of-condition generalization claim; the failed object includes reconstructed input and response mapping, not decision dynamics alone.

claim: The experiment provides choice, response-time and no-response constraints during motion discrimination with scheduled directional perturbations.
note: Descriptive design and behavior; 5 s is an analysis cutoff, not a universal task deadline.

claim: Stimulus reconstruction defines the model input and exposes assumptions and replay uncertainty beyond nominal coherence.
note: Pure reconstruction/input-assumption claim; the unresolved hidden-coherence association is demoted to the supplement. Replay is not a frame-perfect display record.

claim: Joint held-out prediction of control-trial choices, response probabilities and response times favors the tested accumulator among the tested implementations.
note: The joint score is not decomposed into independent successes and is not a population p value.

claim: Randomized signed pulse assignment shifts response direction, and the cumulative response-associated contrast emerges mainly 0.5–2 s after logged onset.
note: Exploratory common-support estimand; timing describes emitted responses, not evidence persistence or a physical-frame timestamp.

claim: At the group level, the tested model-and-input pipelines predict a different temporal profile from the observed pulse-associated response contrast.
note: Descriptive group profile comparison; no paired inferential test of model-minus-observed differences is claimed.

claim: The original and gain-revised predictive gates failed, pulse outcomes did not distinguish the tested strategies with adequate sensitivity, and the confirmatory timing test was not run.
note: Mandatory negative/inconclusive record; low procedural sensitivity is not evidence for absence of primacy.

claim: The data support a relative control-model preference and a directional behavioral pulse effect but do not uniquely identify the sensory, decision or response process that produces the pulse-associated time course.
note: Central scope boundary; the replay and fitted model are treated as one tested prediction pipeline.

claim: In PSUIM6 and PSUIM7, gains chosen to improve held-out pulse choices worsen the remaining response and response-time objective relative to the joint-gain solution.
note: Two-mouse diagnostic subclaim; choices weakly constrain gain in most other mice.

claim: Choice accuracy and temporal-weighting patterns alone do not uniquely distinguish evidence accumulation from tested non-integration, leaky or urgency-based strategies.
note: Model-identification premise; do not generalize beyond the compared strategies.

claim: Joint choice and response-time distributions constrain decision models more strongly than choice accuracy alone.
note: Supports the joint held-out comparison; does not guarantee unique identification.

claim: Brief motion perturbations can affect both choices and response times, but their efficacy depends on pulse timing, commitment and task policy.
note: Motivates pulses while rejecting a context-free mechanistic signature.

claim: The ability of time-varying perturbations to distinguish decision-model implementations depends on prediction separability under the tested noise, timing and response regime.
note: Motivates dataset-specific adequacy and sensitivity calibration without asserting a universal necessary condition.

claim: Sensory dynamics can generate time-dependent behavioral weighting that is inherited by a downstream integrator.
note: Specific sensory-stage alternative; Okazawa supports the broader composite-kernel caveat.

claim: Across several discrete-sample datasets, integration models outperformed tested extrema and snapshot models, although those comparisons did not exhaust possible non-integration policies.
note: Full-text source supports both the positive comparison and its stated scope.

claim: Diffusion models use accuracy and response-time distributions jointly to constrain latent decision and nondecision components.
note: General modeling rationale, not validation of this project's likelihood.

claim: Opponent spatiotemporal motion energy can be constructed from oriented filters and quadrature-pair energy operations.
note: Methods precedent only; does not establish replay fidelity.

claim: Evidence-accumulation parameter estimates should be accompanied by recovery or identifiability checks before mechanistic interpretation.
note: Scoped validation recommendation; the present estimator and model differ.

claim: Mice can perform direction discrimination with continuous noisy random-dot motion.
note: Established mouse RDK precedent; makes no claim about signed pulses or evidence-accumulation mechanism.

claim: Mouse visual accumulation tasks have used stochastic sequences of discrete flashes or visual-tower pulses as the evidence stream.
note: Established dynamic visual-evidence precedent; these events were task evidence rather than perturbations embedded in continuous RDK.

claim: Diffusion decision models have been fitted to mouse visual choices and response-time distributions.
note: Established mouse visual choice/RT modeling precedent; neither is a continuous-RDK pulse-transfer study.
